segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The elder, to the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not I alone but also all who have come to know the truth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because of the truth that remains in us and will be with us forever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace, mercy, and peace will be with us from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Father’s Son, in truth and love.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in truth, just as we received a command from the Father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And now I ask you, lady, not as though I were writing you a new command, but the one we have had from the beginning: that we love one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is love: that we walk according to his commands. This is the command, just as you heard from the beginning, that you walk in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the antichrist.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we worked for, but receive a full reward.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone who goes on ahead and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God. The one who remains in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home, and do not give him a greeting,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for whoever gives him a greeting shares in his evil deeds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Though I have much to write to you, I did not want to do it with paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and speak face to face, so that your joy may be complete.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The children of your chosen sister greet you.

notes.note: ‘Elect’ has become a technical theological term in English; the Greek word is the ordinary adjective for someone picked out or chosen, and the Septuagint uses it of God's chosen people. Most scholars think the ‘lady’ is a figure for a local congregation and her ‘children’ its members, with the ‘chosen sister’ of verse 13 a sister congregation. A minority take her to be an individual woman, and a few read one of the two Greek words as a personal name (Kyria or Electa).

The Greek phrase has no article and could simply mean ‘truly, sincerely’. Because the letter immediately goes on to speak of ‘the truth’ as something known and lasting, many interpreters hear the fuller sense here too: love within the sphere of the truth. ‘In truth’ leaves both readings open, and the same phrase is rendered the same way in verses 3 and 4.

The traditional ‘abide’ is now archaic. The Greek verb is the everyday word for staying or remaining somewhere, and it is rendered ‘remain’ here and in verse 9 so that the repetition can be seen. Several modern translations do the same or use ‘lives’ or ‘continues’.

The Greek pronoun ‘it’ is feminine and could refer to the command, to love, or less probably to truth. Many commentators think love is meant, so that the command is to walk in love. The English keeps the pronoun and leaves the reference open as the Greek does.

notes.traditional: is come in the flesh / has come in the flesh
notes.note: The Greek has a present participle, ‘coming’, whereas the parallel statement in 1 John 4:2 uses a perfect, ‘has come’. Most scholars take the present as a timeless description of the incarnation, which is why many translations write ‘has come’. A minority think it refers to Christ's future return in bodily form. The rendering keeps the present tense and does not decide the question.

notes.traditional: what we have worked for / what you have worked for
notes.note: Manuscripts are divided between ‘what we worked for’ and ‘what you worked for’, and later copies make all three verbs first person (‘that we lose not… but that we receive’), as in the King James Version. The SBLGNT reads ‘we’ for this verb only, meaning the labour of the elder and his fellow teachers. Critical editions and modern translations differ on the point.

The earliest manuscripts have a verb meaning to go ahead or lead the way, which may be an ironic jab at teachers who claimed to be advanced. Later manuscripts replace it with a verb meaning ‘transgress’, which is the source of the King James rendering. Modern editions and translations follow the earlier reading.

notes.traditional: the doctrine of Christ / the teaching of Christ
notes.note: The phrase can mean the teaching that Christ himself gave or the teaching about Christ. Verse 7, which concerns what is confessed about Jesus, favours the second, while John's usual usage of similar phrases favours the first. Scholars are divided, and the English ‘of’ preserves the ambiguity.

Travelling teachers depended on believers for lodging and food, and congregations met in private houses. To receive a teacher into the house was therefore to give him a base and a hearing, and the customary greeting implied welcome and good wishes for his work. The instruction concerns support for those spreading the teaching described in verse 7, not ordinary courtesy toward outsiders.

Manuscripts are divided between ‘your joy’ and ‘our joy’; the two Greek pronouns differ by a single letter and were pronounced alike. The SBLGNT reads ‘your’, while some other critical editions and many translations read ‘our’, as in 1 John 1:4.
